[[Category:Social psychology]]
'''Social loafing''' describes the human tendency to be [[free-rider]]s during a group assignment when

* the outcome is collective,
** particularly, if individual contributions are never identified
* and there is little to no stake.

<ref>{{#cite:Q3470}}</ref>

== Experimental evidence ==

In [[Source:Social Loafing and Expectancy-Value Theory (Scholarly article)|name-author]], 103 participants (35 male, 68 female) were asked to collectively brainstorm the maximum number of uses one can think of a '''knife''' in 15minutes in small groups ($\overline n=4.3,\, \sigma=0.79$), under the following conditions:

* Participants brainstormed in isolated cubicles where they cannot see the progress of their teammates
* Four practice runs on other objects (e.g, shoebox) were conducted before the actual experimental run
* Participants were told that only the number, not quality of ideas would be considered.

Additional per group conditions were imposed:

* '''Instrumentality'''
* Participants were told that the top 10th percentile of the groups in the experimental run would receive either a free pizza or free movie voucher. They received pre-determined false feedback about group-standing during the practice runs.
** '''High instrumentality''': false feedback (90th, 82nd,92nd,84th)
** '''Low instrumentality''': false feedback (86th, 68th, 46th, 49th)
* '''Evaluation/no evaluation''': participants were either told that their individual contributions would be counted, or only the group total would be considered.
* '''Control''': neither evaluation nor instrumentality information

Researchers found with high certainty that:

* '''High instrumentality''' (Knowing that effort would potentially pay off) encourages effort ($p=0.032$);
* '''Evaluation''' (i.e., having individual contributions recognised) increases subjects' engagement when subject [[motivation]] is otherwise low (low instrumentality) ($p=0.028$);
* '''Low instrumentality''' coupled with '''evaluation''' encourages the most effort, a phenomenon as [[social compensation]] ($p<0.001$).
